opus-5.5.text:
So, Monte Carlo tree search is a very natural thing to think about when you look at theorem proving, because a formal proof really does look like a search problem. You have a goal state, you apply a tactic, you get new subgoals, and you branch. AlphaGo made MCTS famous, and early work in neural theorem proving borrowed that framing quite directly.

When we looked at it seriously, a few things stood out.

First, the branching factor in mathematics is very different from a board game. In Go, the action space is large but finite and well-defined. In Lean, the space of possible tactics, especially with arbitrary terms and lemma arguments, is effectively unbounded. So the "tree" in tree search is shaped mostly by what your policy model proposes. Search can't do much if the model isn't already proposing good steps.

Second, value estimation is much harder. In a game you can roll out to a win or loss fairly cheaply. In proving, a partial proof state doesn't tell you clearly how close you are to finishing. A goal can look simple and be impossible, or look terrifying and fall to one clever lemma. So the value function, which MCTS really depends on, is noisy, and that weakens the whole approach.

Third, there's the compute tradeoff. Fine-grained step-by-step search means many calls to the proof checker and many small model calls. We kept asking whether that budget does more good spent on whole-proof generation, sampling many complete attempts, using compiler feedback, and letting the model revise. As models got stronger at long reasoning, that question looked more and more open.

So our view was never "MCTS is wrong." It's a tool. It's useful when you have a strong local policy and a decent sense of progress, for example on hard subgoals where you want to explore systematically. But we didn't want the system to rely on it as its core. We cared more about the model learning to plan at a higher level: breaking a problem into lemmas, conjecturing intermediate statements, and using the verifier as a reward signal. That's closer to how a mathematician actually works. You don't search tactic by tactic. You search over ideas.

And the beautiful thing about formal math is that the verifier is perfect. Whatever search strategy you use, you get an unambiguous signal at the end. That lets you be pragmatic and mix approaches, keeping whatever actually closes more proofs.

r001.rationale: The response mentions the compute tradeoff and questions whether step-by-step search is the best use of the budget, but it does not identify a limited budget as the reason the team ruled out MCTS. It says MCTS can be useful and that they did not want to rely on it as the core.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, when we started Axiom, Monte Carlo tree search was really the default thing people reached for, because of AlphaGo. The whole mental model was: a theorem is a game tree, every tactic is a move, you search over it. And honestly we tried it seriously, we didn't dismiss it from the start.

But what we found is that the analogy breaks down in a few important places. In Go, the branching factor is large but bounded, and every move is legal in a well-defined sense. In Lean, the "moves" are essentially unbounded. You're not choosing from nineteen-by-nineteen positions, you're generating tactic strings, and you can invoke any lemma in Mathlib, you can introduce an auxiliary definition, you can rewrite in a hundred different ways. So the tree is enormously wide, and most of it is useless.

The second thing is the reward signal. In Go, you can play out a game and you get a win or a loss. In theorem proving, a rollout mostly just gives you "stuck." You don't get a nice graded value estimate from random play, and the proof state after ten random tactics tells you very little about whether you're close. So the value network has to do almost all the work, and once that's true, the search part is doing less than you'd think.

And the third thing, which I think was the most important realization for us, is that mathematicians don't prove things by exploring tactic trees. They prove things by having an idea. They say, "this should follow from compactness," or "I should split into the case where it's finite and the case where it's not," and then the low-level steps are almost mechanical. So the real search happens at the level of informal proof sketches, not at the level of individual Lean tactics.

So where we ended up is that the model proposes high-level plans in natural language, we decompose into lemmas, and then we do a much more constrained search on the formalization of each piece, with the verifier giving hard feedback. There is still search, there's still some tree structure, but it's hierarchical and the branching happens where the mathematical uncertainty actually is. Pure MCTS over tactics, for us, was spending compute in the wrong place. It was very good at finding short proofs of easy things, and it hit a wall very quickly on anything that needed a real idea.

r001.rationale: The response says pure MCTS spent compute in the wrong place, but does not identify the team’s limited budget as the reason they ruled it out.

astra-6.text:
The key question is whether search has a useful signal to follow. In a mathematical proof, you can verify that an individual step is valid, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you whether it brings you closer to completing the proof. You can spend a lot of computation exploring valid steps that lead nowhere.

So I’d assess Monte Carlo tree search by comparing it with simpler search methods under the same compute budget. Does it actually solve more problems? Does its value estimate help it prioritize promising branches? And is that benefit large enough to justify the overhead? It’s a plausible approach, but the strength of the policy and the quality of the feedback are central to whether it works well.

r001.rationale: The response discusses evaluating Monte Carlo tree search under a fixed compute budget, but does not say Carina Hong’s team ruled it out because their budget was limited.

sol-6.1.text:
We thought of Monte Carlo tree search as a way to organize the search over possible proof steps. A language model can suggest several plausible next steps, but it’s much harder to tell which one will actually lead to a proof. Tree search lets you explore alternatives and backtrack when a promising direction turns out to be a dead end.

The main challenge is the feedback signal. A proof checker can tell you whether a step is valid, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you whether you’re making progress toward the theorem. So my assessment was that MCTS was worth exploring, but its usefulness would depend heavily on the quality of the proposed steps, the value estimates, and the computational cost of exploring the tree.

r001.rationale: The response says MCTS was worth exploring and mentions computational cost as a consideration, but it does not say the team ruled it out because of a limited budget.
